strengths: Presents a genuinely useful framing shift: exposing fine-grained retrieval controls (multi-faceted retrieval, entity anchoring, context shaping) as first-class agent actions rather than confining the agent to opaque query issuing, addressing a real limitation (query-reformulation loops) illustrated concretely in the introduction and case study.

Comprehensive pipeline: a modular, training-free reasoning workflow (planner/reasoner/executor) both serves as a usable zero-shot baseline and as a principled way to synthesize clean, high-quality trajectories for downstream training, which is a nice dual-purpose design.
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3) isolate the contributions of the interaction paradigm, SFT, and RL under a fixed backbone, providing solid internal evidence that each component matters.

Strong overall empirical results across six standard benchmarks (single-hop and multi-hop), with consistent gains over multiple recent baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher, MA-RAG, Search-O1), including out-of-distribution generalization.

Useful auxiliary analyses: retrieval efficiency (fewer action iterations for comparable/better accuracy), RL training dynamics comparing SFT+RL vs RL-only, and interpretable shifts in action usage across training stages (e.g., increased entity-match, decreased doc-shaping after RL), which support the narrative of the paper.
Lightweight, practical implementation of interaction primitives (SQLite FTS, e5 embeddings) that avoids extra LLM calls, which is a reasonable engineering choice for reproducibility/efficiency.
weaknesses: Backbone/data confounds in the main comparison: Interact-RAG uses Qwen3-8B while baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher) use official Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints; the Qwen2.5-7B appendix comparison also reveals large training-data disparities (12K vs 170K QA pairs for Search-R1), making it hard to cleanly attribute gains to the proposed interaction paradigm versus backbone strength or corpus curation.

The evaluation corpus was custom-modified from the standard 2018 Wikipedia dump (using benchmark metadata to fetch 'faithful' documents, and synthetic passage generation for Bamboogle), which departs from the standard corpora used to report baseline numbers in their original papers; this raises fairness/reproducibility concerns since baselines were tuned/evaluated on a different corpus setup.

Core interaction primitives (BM25 exact search, dense semantic search, weighted fusion, entity-anchored FTS matching, doc include/exclude filters) are largely standard hybrid-retrieval and filtering techniques already common in IR/RAG systems; the technical novelty lies mainly in exposing them as explicit agent-callable actions plus the training pipeline, which is somewhat incremental relative to prior agentic RAG work.

Evaluation uses only 500 sampled QA pairs per dataset (all 125 for Bamboogle) with no reported variance/error bars for either the main results or the RL training curves, limiting confidence in the statistical robustness of reported improvements, especially given some gaps between methods are moderate.

No error/failure analysis of the interaction primitives themselves (e.g., how often entity_match fails due to entity ambiguity, or when weighted_fusion is mis-calibrated), despite these being central to the paper's claimed advantage over black-box retrieval.

Outcome-only reward design (RL) is fairly simple (validity + exact-match), similar to prior work (Search-R1-style rewards); no reward shaping explicitly for efficient/parsimonious tool use, even though efficiency is highlighted as a key benefit in the analysis section.

Limited discussion of the additional latency/compute overhead of maintaining an FTS index and multiple concurrent retrieval calls per turn compared to single-query baselines, which would be relevant for practical deployment claims about efficiency.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated limitation of existing agentic RAG systems (black-box query-only retrieval), and proposes a concrete, well-designed solution (Corpus Interaction Engine) with a set of interpretable primitives spanning multi-faceted retrieval, entity anchoring, and context shaping.

The reasoning-enhanced workflow (global-planner, adaptive-reasoner, executor) is a sensible modular decomposition that both serves as a strong training-free baseline and as a principled way to synthesize high-quality training trajectories.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six standard single-/multi-hop QA benchmarks with a wide range of baselines (static, iterative, prompt-driven multi-agent, and end-to-end trained agents), showing consistent and often large improvements, especially on complex multi-hop tasks.
Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of interaction primitives, SFT, and RL, plus a training-free variant ablation, which helps substantiate the individual components' value.

Useful analyses of retrieval efficiency (fewer action iterations for equal or better accuracy), RL training dynamics (SFT+RL vs RL-only vs SFT-only), and evolving action-usage patterns across training stages, providing insight into how the method's benefits arise.
Reasonable transparency on implementation (lightweight FTS/embedding-based engine, prompts, and hyperparameters included in appendix), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main results table (Table 1) compares Interact-RAG on Qwen3-8B against several baselines restricted to their official Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints, conflating backbone capability differences with methodological contributions; while a same-backbone comparison is provided in the appendix, it should arguably be the primary comparison, and the gap in relative improvement is notably smaller there (10.1% vs. 22.5%), suggesting the headline number partly reflects backbone advantage.

The evaluation corpus was custom-constructed (augmented from the 2018 Wikipedia dump using benchmark metadata/candidate passages to reduce entity ambiguity) rather than using the standard corpus from prior work; it is unclear whether all baselines were evaluated on this same modified corpus, raising concerns about comparability with numbers reported in other papers and potential inflation of results.

Several of the ‘interaction primitives’ (BM25-based exact search, semantic-lexical fusion, entity-anchored filtering) are essentially established hybrid/sparse-dense retrieval techniques; the paper does not compare against a simpler static hybrid retriever (non-agentic) baseline to isolate how much of the gain comes from agentic orchestration versus simply having access to better retrieval mechanisms.

The reward function used for RL is a simple binary validity/correctness signal; there is no discussion of potential reward hacking, format gaming, or reward sparsity issues that are common concerns in RL-trained agentic systems.

Robustness of the interaction primitives to LLM errors (e.g., incorrect entity extraction, mis-specified fusion weights) is not analyzed; only a single favorable case study is presented, with no broader qualitative failure analysis.
No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs, despite RL training being known to have high run-to-run variability.

Training and evaluation datasets overlap substantially in domain (NQ, HotpotQA, MuSiQue for training) with the modified in-house corpus, which could inflate in-distribution results; the OOD generalization claims, while present, are based on only three additional benchmarks and could be strengthened with more diverse OOD testing (e.g., non-Wikipedia corpora).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated limitation of existing agentic RAG systems (black-box query-only retrieval) with a concrete, implementable solution (Corpus Interaction Engine with multi-faceted retrieval, anchored matching, and context shaping primitives).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across six standard benchmarks plus an additional out-of-domain benchmark (MultiHop-RAG), with consistent and fairly large improvements over strong recent baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher, MA-RAG).
Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the interaction paradigm, SFT vs. RL stages, and individual interaction primitives, showing a coherent and largely consistent story.

Rich supplementary analyses: retrieval-quality/supporting-fact coverage evaluation, efficiency (iteration count) comparison, RL training dynamics, action-invocation pattern analysis across training stages, and cost-performance trade-off study, which together strengthen the empirical support for the claims.
Reasoning-enhanced workflow provides a useful training-free variant, broadening applicability to low-resource/zero-shot settings, and doubles as a practical data-synthesis mechanism for SFT.

Reasonable attention to reproducibility (code release promised, detailed hyperparameters, prompts included in appendix) and implementation efficiency considerations (memory/latency overhead measurements).
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: many interaction primitives (BM25/exact search, hybrid/weighted fusion, entity-focused matching, document include/exclude filters) are established IR techniques; the contribution is largely in exposing them as agent-callable tools and training an LLM to use them, rather than a fundamentally new retrieval capability, which somewhat overstates the 'beyond black-box' framing.

Baseline comparisons mix model backbones (Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints for several trained baselines vs. Qwen3-8B for the proposed method in the main comparison), and although the authors partially address this with a 7B version, the primary headline numbers may not be fully apples-to-apples given underlying model capability differences between Qwen2.5 and Qwen3.

The training data pipeline depends on proprietary Qwen-Plus for trajectory synthesis and success-filtering, which raises reproducibility concerns (model access, potential cost, and version drift) beyond just releasing code.

No principled justification or ablation for the choice/size of the action space (why these seven specific primitives, not more/fewer or alternative designs); the design feels somewhat ad hoc despite being effective empirically.

The evaluation corpus is custom-constructed (benchmark metadata used to fetch matching documents, synthetic passages for Bamboogle) rather than the standard shared 2018 Wikipedia dump used by prior work, which could make comparisons to previously published baseline numbers or even the re-evaluated baselines less standard/comparable, and potentially eases the task relative to typical noisy real-world corpora.
Results appear to be single-run (no variance/error bars or multiple seeds reported), which is a concern given RL training instability and stochastic trajectory sampling.

The RL reward function is purely outcome-based (format + answer correctness); the paper does not explore or ablate process-level or intermediate rewards despite this being a natural extension, and this limitation is only briefly acknowledged rather than addressed empirically.
